rv.q: Dominic Cooke’s production rewires the drama so that its historical importance is shown, its autobiographical element made vivid, its currency made vivacious.

Ultimately though, Cooke’s production is a rejuvenation.

His thoughtful revamp of Emlyn Williams's semi-autobiographical 1938 work The Corn is Green, about the schoolteacher who changed his destiny, throbs with new life and features a powerhouse turn from Nicola Walker.

Yes, this play has dated and, though no doubt dear to its author, not his best work, but Emlyn Williams has been off our stages for too long and, despite its faults, this is still a good night in the theatre.

This is not a great play and it’s presented as a larky excuse to mock stereotypes that died out 70 years ago.
DOMINIC Cooke’s buoyant production of Emlyn Williams’ play is unashamedly feel-good theatre. First produced in 1938, The Corn is Green’s themes may feel dated but this revival is utterly absorbing.
Dominic Cooke refreshes this Pygmalion meets Dead Poets Society tale with an entertaining metatheatrical spin.

cn.t: Cooke's imaginative revival breathes fresh life into Williams' 1938 play, with Walker delivering a powerhouse performance as the inspirational teacher. Critics mostly praise its entertaining, affecting qualities, though some find it dated and overly sentimental.
